newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peronists to obey labor decree freeze but fight on.
newsitem.headline: Peronists to obey labor decree freeze but fight on.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem will not appeal a court decision to freeze his decrees on labor reforms, but will defend their legitimacy, Justice Minister Elias Jassan said Wednesday.

Menem's attempts to tackle Argentina's high unemployment of 17.3 percent via "labor flexibilization" -- or loosening up labor legislation -- by decree have tripped on court rulings that they are unconstitutional and must be suspended.
The Peronist president does, however, plan to appeal the ruling of 10 days ago that his decrees violate the constitution, and also wants 77-year-old Labor Judge Julio Garcia Martinez impeached.

But he has decided to comply with Monday's ruling by Labor Judge Ines Gassibe that suspends the decrees pending a fuller explanation of them by the government. She was acting on a petition by the main CGT trade union federation.
"The government is going to defend the legitimacy of the decrees in the court where they have been questioned," Jassan told reporters after talks with the president.

Menem resorted to decrees in the face of opposition to his labor reforms in Congress and a breakdown in negotiations with unions, who fear their power is under threat. The CGT staged a 24-hour general strike on December 26, its third in the year.

His Peronist government had been working on another batch of decrees to follow up the first three, which allow workers to choose their union health plan, let smaller firms bypass national unions in collective pay talks and let firms appeal to the government if they want to negotiate with unions on a company-by-company and not an industry-wide basis.

Menem's ministers slammed Judge Garcia Martinez's ruling as a "political" maneuver and dismissed it on the technicality that the ruling was made on a court holiday and the government was not informed. One senior aide threatened to have the second judge impeached as well, but that threat has faded.

The CGT has called Menem's attempt to rule by decree a sign of "impotence" and the Radical and Frepaso opposition parties accused him of "authoritarianism" for responding with impeachment threats to judges who question his decrees.

But CGT chief Rodolfo Daer decided Tuesday to return to the negotiating table with the government, though he demanded that talks deal with "all issues and not just flexibilization which the government wants and which we reject."
